newsitem.title: UK: Smaller UK stocks shut out of blue-chip party.
newsitem.headline: Smaller UK stocks shut out of blue-chip party.

text.p: For British equities this year, big has been beautiful.

Britain's blue-chips have had an exuberant 1997, with the FTSE 100 index waltzing to a series of record highs, fuelled by a cocktail of stock shortages, bid speculation and a flood of institutional buying.
Smaller stocks, meanwhile, have been left shut out of the party.

The FTSE SmallCap index has only managed to crawl one percent higher since the start of the year, while the FTSE 250 index of mid-cap stocks has actually slipped back a handful of points from its end-1996 close.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index climbed 20 percent over the same period.

Yet some analysts believe the fortunes of smaller-cap stocks may soon be about to change. Simon Smith, head of UK equities at fund managers Albert E Sharp, expects the smaller companies market to start climbing in September and outperform the FTSE 100 through the next year.

"We believe that in September, when everyone returns to their desks, fund managers' attention will turn to smaller companies which we believe will outperform the main indexes significantly in the coming 12 months," Smith said.
"At this stage of the economic cycle, smaller companies have traditionally stood on premium ratings," he said.
"Today they are at significant discounts. Thus the main market either looks expensive or, as we believe, the smaller companies market looks significantly undervalued."

Two factors in particular have stifled growth for smaller-cap stocks, analysts say -- they have been largely ignored by the institutions which have poured cash into blue-chip stocks, and they have been badly dented by the strength of sterling.
But Smith said the wost of the damage done by sterling's strength was already out of the way.
"Sterling's strength, which made the early part of the year so difficult, may now be close to peaking," he said.

"Companies are learning to live with sterling at these levels and exporters, which led the economy out of recession in the early 1990s, look set to perform a lot better for the remainder of the decade."
He said the fundamantal picture remained convincing for smaller-cap stocks, and the consumer recovey remained firm.
Not all strategists are so convinced, however.
Analysts at BZW believe the impact of Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown's July 2 budget will keep shares in smaller companies under pressure.
"The specific implications of Gordon Brown's first budget -- higher rates, higher taxes and higher sterling -- are likely to dominate the equity market throughout the summer," BZW said.
"Mid-cap and small-cap stocks, which are almost in a bear market already, look set to bear the burden of this uncomfortable post-budget policy mix."

Smaller stocks seemed likely to remain relatively friendless, the brokerage said. "While the valuation of the FTSE 100 does look a bit rich, its relative insulation to these pressures makes it the more likely recipient of the surplus liquidity around."
